questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 10 days. Dark-field microscopy of the serous exudate shows motile spiral organisms. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (chancre) caused by Treponema pallidum is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose — first-line per WHO and CDC guidelines. Doxycycline is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with photosensitive butterfly rash. She has oral ulcers and malar erythema sparing the nasolabial folds. Which antibody is MOST specific for this diagnosis?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is highly specific (~99%) for SLE though not very sensitive (~25%). Anti-dsDNA is specific but also seen in other conditions. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus. Anti-Ro/SSA is seen in neonatal lupus and Sjogren's syndrome.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with a chronic ulcer on the right foot with draining sinuses discharging white sulfur granules. KOH mount shows large fungal elements and granules. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Madura foot (mycetoma) with black/dark-colored granules suggests Madurella mycetomatis (eumycetoma). White/pale granules can suggest Actinomadura madurae (actinomycetoma). The presence of large fungal elements on KOH points to eumycetoma. Madurella mycetomatis is the most common cause of black-grain eumycetoma in India.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a tense bulla on erythematous base on the trunk. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) presents with tense bullae on an urticarial base in older adults. Nikolsky sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 along BMZ (hemidesmosomes – BP180 and BP230 antigens). Pemphigus vulgaris shows intraepidermal acantholysis with positive Nikolsky sign and IgG/C3 in intercellular pattern.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with hypopigmented anesthetic patches on the trunk and thickening of the ulnar nerve at elbow. Slit skin smear is negative. Skin biopsy shows epithelioid granulomas with giant cells and lymphocytic infiltration. What type of leprosy is this?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) presents with few well-defined hypopigmented anesthetic patches, enlarged peripheral nerves, and negative SSS (paucibacillary). Biopsy shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells and lymphocytic cuffing. Strong cell-mediated immunity controls the bacillary load.

questions.q: A 32-year-old HIV-positive man presents with multiple painless ulcers on the perianal region, inguinal lymphadenopathy, and rectal discharge. Serology shows LGV-specific antibodies. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3 is treated with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days. Erythromycin is an alternative. Azithromycin is used for uncomplicated chlamydia (1g single dose), not LGV.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops tightening of the skin over the fingers, Raynaud's phenomenon, and telangiectasias. ANA is positive with anticentromere pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) is limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Anticentromere antibody (ACA) is highly specific for limited SSc/CREST. Diffuse SSc is associated with anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I).

questions.q: A 19-year-old presents with painful vesicles on an erythematous base along the T5 dermatome. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. Which antiviral agent is most appropriate for treatment?
opts: Acyclovir 200 mg 5 times daily for 5 days
Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Herpes zoster (VZV reactivation) is treated with acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days, or valacyclovir 1000 mg TDS for 7 days, or famciclovir 500 mg TDS for 7 days. Acyclovir 200 mg 5 times daily is the dose for primary herpes simplex, not zoster.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with well-demarcated silvery scaly plaques on the extensor surfaces of elbows and knees. Auspitz sign is positive. Skin biopsy would most characteristically show:
opts: Acanthosis with parakeratosis and neutrophilic infiltration in stratum corneum (Munro microabscesses)
Interface dermatitis with basal vacuolar degeneration
questions.exp: Psoriasis histopathology shows regular acanthosis (psoriasiform hyperplasia), parakeratosis, thinning of the suprapapillary plate, dilated dermal capillaries, and Munro microabscesses (neutrophilic collections in stratum corneum). Kogoj's spongiform pustules are seen in pustular psoriasis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a pearly nodule with rolled borders and telangiectasias on the nose. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels. What is the most appropriate primary treatment for a 1.5 cm lesion on the nose?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose is a high-risk location (H-zone) requiring Mohs micrographic surgery for complete margin assessment and maximum tissue conservation. Mohs has the highest cure rate for high-risk BCCs. Standard excision may miss subclinical extension in nasal BCC.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions on the face around the mouth and nose. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which organism is MOST commonly responsible?
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is classically caused by Staphylococcus aureus (most common), though Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A strep) can also be causative. Honey-colored crusts on the face in a child is the classic presentation. Gram-positive cocci in clusters = staphylococci.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman is being treated with dapsone for leprosy and develops sudden onset pallor, jaundice, and fatigue. CBC shows Hb 6 g/dL with reticulocytosis and Heinz bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Dapsone-induced hemolytic anemia due to G6PD deficiency
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent hemolytic anemia, which is more severe in G6PD-deficient individuals. Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin precipitates) are characteristic. Dapsone also causes methemoglobinemia. All patients starting dapsone should be screened for G6PD deficiency. Agranulocytosis is a rare but serious side effect.

questions.q: A patient presents with erythema, scaling, and pruritus in the beard area with follicular pustules. KOH mount shows hyphae penetrating the hair shaft. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tinea barbae (ringworm of the beard) is a dermatophyte infection of the beard region in men, causing inflammatory follicular pustules, erythema, and crusting. KOH shows fungal hyphae. It is most commonly caused by Trichophyton verrucosum or T. mentagrophytes (zoophilic). Pseudofolliculitis barbae is caused by ingrown hairs, not fungi.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules with Wickham's striae on the flexor aspects of the wrists. Oral mucosa shows a reticular white pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lichen planus classic presentation: 4 Ps — Pruritic, Purple (violaceous), Polygonal, Papules on flexor wrists. Wickham's striae (lacy white lines) are pathognomonic. Oral LP shows reticular pattern. DIF shows saw-tooth pattern of IgG, C3, fibrin at BMZ. Colloid (Civatte) bodies are seen on histology.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging ulcerated lesion on the lower lip with raised everted borders and regional lymphadenopathy. He is a chronic pipe smoker. Biopsy shows islands of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls. What is the staging workup modality of choice for lymph node assessment?
questions.exp: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lip with regional LN involvement requires PET-CT for comprehensive staging, including detection of distant metastases and occult nodal disease. PET-CT is superior to CT/MRI for nodal staging in head and neck SCC. FNAC is useful for cytological confirmation but not for staging.

questions.q: During a Mohs micrographic surgery, frozen sections are processed en face (horizontal) and examined. The primary advantage of this technique over standard excision with paraffin sections is:
opts: Faster turnaround time allowing same-day completion
Examination of 100% of the surgical margin compared to ~1% with standard sections
questions.exp: The key advantage of Mohs surgery is complete circumferential peripheral and deep margin assessment — essentially 100% of the surgical margin is examined. Standard bread-loaf sections examine only ~1% of the margin, risking undetected positive margins. This results in the highest cure rates for skin cancers in high-risk locations.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent oral and genital ulcers, a positive pathergy test, and uveitis. What is the diagnosis and what is the HLA association?
questions.exp: Behcet's disease (BD) presents with recurrent painful oral aphthae, genital ulcers, ocular inflammation (uveitis), and skin lesions (pathergy, pseudofolliculitis). Pathergy test (hyperreactivity to minor trauma) is characteristic. BD has a strong association with HLA-B51, especially in endemic regions (Silk Road countries). Reiter's/reactive arthritis is associated with HLA-B27.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer from Maharashtra presents with painless ulcer on the dorsum of the hand with satellite lesions and regional lymphadenopathy. Sporotrichosis is suspected. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Sporothrix schenckii infection (cutaneous/lymphocutaneous type) is treated with itraconazole 100-200 mg/day for 3-6 months — now the preferred first-line treatment per IDSA guidelines. SSKI (saturated solution of potassium iodide) was the traditional treatment but is less used now due to side effects. Amphotericin B is reserved for disseminated or severe disease.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with pruritic vesicles on the elbows, knees, and buttocks in a symmetric distribution. She has recently been diagnosed with celiac disease. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillae. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is strongly associated with celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). Presents with intensely pruritic vesiculopapules on extensor surfaces. DIF of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits in dermal papillae — pathognomonic. Linear IgA disease shows linear IgA along the BMZ. Treatment: dapsone + gluten-free diet.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with a well-demarcated patch of hair loss on the scalp. The hairs at the margin show a 'exclamation mark' appearance. No scarring is present. What is the pathophysiology of this condition?
opts: Miniaturization of hair follicles due to androgen sensitivity
Autoimmune T-cell mediated attack on the hair bulb
Fungal invasion of the hair shaft
questions.exp: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition where CD8+ cytotoxic T cells attack the hair follicle bulb, causing immune-privilege collapse. The pathognomonic 'exclamation mark' hairs (tapered at the base) are found at the periphery of active patches. It is non-scarring (follicles preserved). Associated with other autoimmune diseases (thyroid, vitiligo).

questions.q: A 58-year-old man on long-term hydroxyurea for CML develops melanonychia, leg ulcers, and hyperpigmentation. Which mechanism best explains the mucocutaneous side effects of hydroxyurea?
opts: Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase causing folate deficiency
Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase causing DNA repair defects and UV sensitivity
Inhibition of topoisomerase II causing chromosomal instability
questions.exp: Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, impairing DNA synthesis and repair. Chronic use causes several mucocutaneous changes: melanonychia, longitudinal melanonychia, hyperpigmentation, leg ulcers (especially over malleoli), oral ulcers, and dermatomyositis-like eruption. Photosensitivity can also occur. These are not folate-related.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man presents with a painless nodule on the glans penis that has been present for 6 months. Biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal dysplasia without invasion. He is uncircumcised. What is this condition called?
questions.exp: Erythroplasia of Queyrat (EQ) is squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the glans penis or prepuce in uncircumcised men, presenting as a velvety erythematous plaque. It shows full-thickness epidermal dysplasia on histology. Bowenoid papulosis presents with multiple pigmented papules, often HPV-related, on the shaft. EQ has ~10-30% risk of invasion.

questions.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman (28 weeks gestation) presents with intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques on the abdomen, sparing the umbilicus. The rash started in the striae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP/PUPP — pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy) is the most common pregnancy dermatosis. It starts in abdominal striae, characteristically SPARES the umbilicus, and appears in the third trimester. It is benign with no fetal risk. Pemphigoid gestationis begins periumbilically with blistering and has DIF-positive perilesional skin (linear C3/IgG).

questions.q: A 25-year-old man from a leprosy-endemic region presents with sudden onset shiny erythema over a pre-existing hypopigmented patch and mild fever. The patch is now erythematous and edematous. Slit skin smear is negative. What is this reaction called and which cytokine is primarily responsible?
questions.exp: Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction) is a delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) reaction occurring in borderline leprosy. Existing lesions become erythematous, edematous, and inflamed. It is driven by a sudden increase in cell-mediated immunity with IFN-γ as the primary cytokine. ENL (Type 2) is an immune complex-mediated reaction (Type III) driven by TNF-α, occurring in BL/LL leprosy.

questions.q: A 12-year-old child presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the lip recurring 3-4 times per year, triggered by sunlight and fever. Viral culture grows HSV-1. What is the mechanism of viral latency?
opts: Virus integrates into the host genome at the epidermal keratinocyte level
Virus remains dormant in the dorsal root ganglion as circular episomal DNA
Virus is eliminated after primary infection but reinfection occurs from external sources
Virus maintains a persistent low-level replication in oral mucosal epithelium
questions.exp: HSV establishes latency in sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia (trigeminal ganglion for oral HSV-1, sacral ganglia for genital HSV-2) as non-integrated episomal DNA. LAT (latency-associated transcripts) maintain latency. Reactivation occurs due to UV exposure, fever, stress, immunosuppression, causing recurrent outbreaks along the sensory nerve distribution.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman on methotrexate for psoriasis develops mouth ulcers, nausea, and macrocytic anemia after 3 weeks of treatment. What is the mechanism of this toxicity and how should it be managed?
opts: Hepatotoxicity — add ursodeoxycholic acid and reduce dose
Folate antagonism — add folic acid 5 mg/week (not on same day as MTX)
Renal accumulation — increase fluid intake and alkalinize urine
Bone marrow suppression due to direct alkylation — give G-CSF
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), depleting tetrahydrofolate required for DNA synthesis and purine/thymidylate synthesis. This causes mucositis, cytopenias, and GI toxicity. Folic acid supplementation 5 mg/week (given 1-2 days apart from MTX) reduces toxicity without compromising efficacy. Folinic acid (leucovorin) is used in overdose/severe toxicity.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a rapidly growing pigmented lesion on the back that has developed over 6 weeks. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network, blue-white veil, regression structures, and irregular streaks. Biopsy shows vertical growth phase melanoma with Breslow thickness 2.5 mm and mitotic rate 3/mm². What is the standard sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) indication?
opts: Breslow thickness >0.8 mm OR any thickness with ulceration/mitotic rate ≥1/mm²
Any melanoma regardless of Breslow thickness
Only for Breslow thickness >4 mm (T4 stage)
Only if clinical lymphadenopathy is present
questions.exp: SLNB is indicated per current guidelines for melanomas >0.8 mm Breslow thickness, or T1b melanomas (0.8-1.0 mm with adverse features OR any thickness with ulceration). This patient (2.5 mm Breslow, mitotic rate 3/mm²) clearly qualifies. SLNB provides important staging information; a positive SLN guides further management including completion LND and adjuvant therapy.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with multiple firm skin-colored nodules on the trunk since childhood. Examination reveals 8 cafe-au-lait macules >1.5 cm diameter and axillary freckling. His father has a similar condition. Which gene is mutated in this autosomal dominant condition?
questions.exp: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1/von Recklinghausen's disease) is caused by mutations in NF1 gene on chromosome 17q11.2, encoding neurofibromin (a RAS-GAP tumor suppressor). Diagnostic criteria: ≥6 CALMs (>1.5 cm in post-pubertal), ≥2 neurofibromas, axillary/inguinal freckling (Crowe's sign), optic glioma, Lisch nodules, first-degree relative with NF1.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with patchy depigmentation of the face, hands, and genitalia. Wood's lamp examination shows chalk-white fluorescence. Dermoscopy shows perifollicular pigmentation and follicular openings. Which finding on dermoscopy suggests a BETTER prognosis for repigmentation?
opts: Diffuse white fluorescence without follicular structures
questions.exp: In vitiligo, perifollicular repigmentation on dermoscopy (speckled/follicular pattern) indicates that melanocyte stem cells in the outer root sheath of hair follicles are intact, suggesting better response to treatment. Follicular repigmentation is the most common and favorable pattern. Complete absence of follicular structures suggests total melanocyte loss and poorer prognosis.

questions.q: A 38-year-old man presents with erythematous scaly plaques in the scalp, nasolabial folds, and eyebrows. He also has similar lesions on the presternal region. The condition flares in winter. Malassezia furfur is implicated. What is the first-line topical treatment?
questions.exp: Seborrheic dermatitis (SD) is an inflammatory condition triggered by Malassezia yeasts. First-line treatment is topical antifungal agents (ketoconazole 2%, selenium sulfide, zinc pyrithione, ciclopirox) in shampoo or cream formulations. Topical corticosteroids are used adjunctively for short-term anti-inflammatory effect. Tacrolimus is a second-line option for steroid-sparing therapy.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with itchy papules on the finger webs, wrists, and genitalia, worse at night. His roommate has similar symptoms. Dermoscopy shows the 'delta-wing jet with contrail' sign (jet sign). Microscopic examination of skin scrapings shows the causative organism. Which drug, if used as a single topical application, is effective for this condition?
opts: Permethrin 5% cream — applied for 8-14 hours, single application
Sulfur 6% ointment applied for 3 consecutive nights
questions.exp: Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei var hominis) is effectively treated with permethrin 5% cream applied from neck downward, left for 8-14 hours, then washed off — a single application is highly effective (>95%). Permethrin acts on the parasite's sodium channels. The 'jet sign' on dermoscopy represents the scabies mite burrow. Ivermectin oral (not topical) is also effective as a single dose.
